content.content:
3. The SystemHost¶
In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root:
```
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
```
The noun is sys, not int, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: OrderFlow
kebab-cases to order-flow, the system's name.
The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with -s topic=orders, in
.intropy/scaffold.json — and sys create scans the workspace for those records and assembles
them into a typed declaration:
```
system-host/
├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
├── Order.cs                      # the contract type the orders topic carries
├── Properties/
│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
```
One thing is conspicuously absent: a dapr-components/ directory. The system's components are not
files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
watches that happen.
One entry point, two backends¶
system-host/Program.cs
```
using System.Reflection;
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```
Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.
The declaration¶
Open Topics.cs. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
system-host/Topics.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```
OrderFlowSystem.cs is the topology itself:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```
Nothing in these files is new information. AddExtractor and AddLoader name the blueprints you
scaffolded; "pubsub" and "orders" are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What sys create did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.
Three things about the shape:
A topic is a value, not a string typed twice: Topics.Orders is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
The edge is derived: no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching Topics.Orders is the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
Block kinds surface at the host: the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  Publishes but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
And one thing about what is not declared: a pub/sub registration. Topics.Orders names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.
Order, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries. The scaffold generates it as a
minimal record next to Topics.cs. It documents the contract at the declaration site and gives
schema-aware tooling something to reflect on; the wiring itself only uses the names.
Declared, then enforced¶
A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and Build() is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run check, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.
Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```
```
dotnet run -- check
```
```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```
Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to Topics.Orders.
How the declaration reaches the code¶
The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.
Info
The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, sys create
assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.
Check it¶
```
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```
```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```
check builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:
```
dotnet run -- graph
```
```
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```
That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.
Recap
sys create assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: Topics.cs defines
  each topic once, OrderFlowSystem.cs wires components to it
The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing Topics.Orders; block kinds at the host
  mirror the blueprints
Build() validates the whole declaration; dotnet run -- check runs the same gate from the
  command line
dotnet run -- graph prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet

```
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```
Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.
The declaration¶
Open Topics.cs. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
system-host/Topics.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```
OrderFlowSystem.cs is the topology itself:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```
Nothing in these files is new information. AddExtractor and AddLoader name the blueprints you
scaffolded; "pubsub" and "orders" are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What sys create did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.

A topic is a value, not a string typed twice: Topics.Orders is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
The edge is derived: no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching Topics.Orders is the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
Block kinds surface at the host: the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  Publishes but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
And one thing about what is not declared: a pub/sub registration. Topics.Orders names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.
Order, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries. The scaffold generates it as a
minimal record next to Topics.cs. It documents the contract at the declaration site and gives
schema-aware tooling something to reflect on; the wiring itself only uses the names.

A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and Build() is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run check, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.
Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```
```
dotnet run -- check
```
```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```
Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to Topics.Orders.
How the declaration reaches the code¶
The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.
Info
The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, sys create
assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.
Check it¶
```
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```
```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```
check builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:
```
dotnet run -- graph
```
```
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```
That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.
Recap
sys create assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: Topics.cs defines
  each topic once, OrderFlowSystem.cs wires components to it
The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing Topics.Orders; block kinds at the host
  mirror the blueprints
Build() validates the whole declaration; dotnet run -- check runs the same gate from the
  command line
dotnet run -- graph prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet

content.content:
===== 01-extractor =====
1. The extractor¶
In this chapter you create the system workspace, scaffold the first of its two integrations, and run it alone: a complete integration on its own isolated components, before any system exists.
Scaffold¶
Create the workspace and render the extractor blueprint into it:
```
mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow
intropy int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor
```
order-flow/ is the system workspace: a plain directory that holds the two integrations and, from chapter 3, the SystemHost as siblings. Nothing about it is special. Each integration stays an independent project you could version, test, and deploy on its own.
Two flags deserve a closer look:
-s topic=orders: the pub/sub topic the extractor publishes to. You'll type the same value when scaffolding the loader — each scaffold declares its own half of the contract, and records it (in .intropy/scaffold.json) for the system to assemble in chapter 3.
No empty=true: unlike the transactional tutorial, you keep the blueprint's sample logic. This tutorial is about what happens between integrations, so the insides stay stock.
The scaffold looks like the transactional layout you know, with the extractor's own components:
```
order-extractor/
├── Taskfile.yml                  # task run / build / test
├── docker-compose.yml            # local observability stack — standalone runs only
├── local/
│   ├── dapr-components/
│   │   ├── poll.yaml             # cron binding — sweeps the inbound folder every 5 s
│   │   ├── inbound.yaml          # folder binding — stands in for the source system
│   │   └── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│   └── sample-data/
│       └── sample-order.json
├── src/                          # implemented: sweep inbound, publish to topic, delete source
└── test/
```
The sample logic ships working. On every poll tick it lists the inbound folder, publishes each file's content as a message on topic orders, and deletes the source file. And unlike the transactional integration, which runs once and exits, the extractor keeps running until you stop it — that matters in chapter 5, when you'll drop files in while the whole system is live.
Check it¶
Run the extractor standalone:
```
cd order-extractor
task run
```
The task seeds sample-order.json into the inbound folder and starts the integration under Dapr, with the sidecar loading only local/dapr-components/. Within a poll tick you should see:
```
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Swept 1 file from inbound
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Stop it with Ctrl+C, then confirm the source file is gone:
```
ls local/storage/inbound/
```
The folder is empty: the extractor swept the file, published it, and cleaned up.
Where did the message go? Into the extractor's own in-memory pub/sub — and nothing subscribes there. That's the point of an isolated run: it verifies the extractor's whole job (sweep, publish, clean up) without needing a consumer to exist. Delivery to a consumer is the system's job, and that's chapter 5.
Recap
Created the order-flow workspace; integrations and the SystemHost live in it as siblings
Scaffolded order-extractor from the extractor blueprint with its sample logic intact
Standalone, the sidecar loads only local/dapr-components/: an isolated, in-memory world
The published message intentionally went nowhere — no consumer exists yet
===== 02-loader =====
2. The loader¶
In this chapter you scaffold order-loader, the consuming half of the system, and verify it the way any subscriber is verified in isolation: by publishing through its own sidecar.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root, render the loader blueprint:
```
intropy int create loader -n OrderLoader -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-loader
```
-s topic=orders is the same value you gave the extractor, and typing it twice is deliberate: each integration declares its own half of the contract and stays verifiable alone. Chapter 3 assembles the two halves into one typed declaration — and checks that they meet.
```
order-loader/
├── Taskfile.yml
├── docker-compose.yml
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/
│       ├── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│       └── destination.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the destination system
├── src/                          # implemented: subscribe to topic, deserialize, validate, load
└── test/
```
The sample logic subscribes to orders on pubsub and, for each message, deserializes the order, validates it, and writes {orderId}.json through the destination binding. Like the extractor, it runs until you stop it.
Note that pubsub.yaml here has the same component name as the extractor's — but they are not the same broker. Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.
Publish through the loader's own sidecar¶
A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists inside the loader's sidecar, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and dapr publish --publish-app-id does exactly that.
Start the loader in one terminal:
```
cd order-loader
task run
```
Wait for the subscription to register:
```
== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Check it¶
In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:
```
dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
```
```
Event published successfully
```
The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:
```
cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json
```
```
{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}
```
Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.
Recap
Scaffolded order-loader: subscribes to orders on pubsub, writes each order through the destination binding
A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet
===== 04-component-scoping =====
4. System-scoped components¶
In this chapter you learn how the same integration code loads different Dapr components depending on who starts it: its own local set when run standalone, the system's generated overlay under the SystemHost.
One file you wrote, one the host generates¶
Open the extractor's pub/sub component:
order-extractor/local/dapr-components/pubsub.yaml
```
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.in-memory
  version: v1
```
The system's counterpart is not a file you wrote. There is no dapr-components/ directory in system-host/, and chapter 3's declaration never mentioned Redis. The host derives it: Topics.Orders names a pubsub component called pubsub, so the run backend generates one, backed by Redis because that is what the local run profile provisions:
system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml (generated)
```
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.redis
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: redisHost
      value: localhost:6379
```
Same metadata.name, different spec.type. That shared name is the whole mechanism: application code addresses components by name and never learns which backing is behind it. Whoever starts the sidecar decides which file the name resolves to — and on the system side that file is generated from the topology, so the model you validated in chapter 3 and the YAML the sidecar loads cannot disagree.
The overlay¶
Standalone, you've already seen the answer: task run starts the sidecar with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components, so the integration gets its isolated, in-memory world.
Under the SystemHost, the host stages an effective component set for each integration before starting its sidecar:
Generate the system's components from the topology: one Redis-backed pubsub, because Topics.Orders names it.
Copy everything from the integration's local/dapr-components/.
Overlay the generated components: a generated component with the same metadata.name replaces the local one; new names are added.
Start the sidecar with --resources-path pointing at the staged directory, under system-host/obj/dapr-components/<integration-name>/.
For the extractor that means poll.yaml and inbound.yaml pass through untouched — sweeping a local folder is the integration's own business in both modes — while the local pubsub.yaml is replaced by the generated one.
Why an overlay, rather than handing the sidecar both directories? Because Dapr refuses duplicate component names across resource paths, and the duplicate name is the mechanism. And why not have the host generate a complete set? Then the topology would have to describe every folder binding in every integration — concerns that are the integration's own business, not the system's.
The overlay has edges worth knowing: it is staged when the host starts, so changing the topology means restarting the SystemHost; it keys on metadata.name, not the filename; and a generated component applies to every integration in the system. The Redis port is pinned to 6379, so the YAML above is exactly what the sidecars load. The staged files are real YAML on disk — inspect them whenever resolution surprises you — but editing them is futile: they are regenerated from the model on every start. Change the declaration, not the artifacts.
Check it¶
Start the system for the first time:
```
cd system-host
dotnet run
```
Leave it running and, from the workspace root in a second terminal, inspect what was staged for the extractor:
```
ls system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/
```
```
inbound.yaml  poll.yaml  pubsub.yaml
```
```
grep "type:" system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml
```
```
  type: pubsub.redis
```
The two local components passed through; the pub/sub is now the system's — generated, not written. Stop the host with Ctrl+C — the next chapter runs it for real.
Recap
Component resolution is decided by whoever starts the sidecar: the local directory standalone, the staged overlay under the SystemHost
Local components pass through untouched; a generated component with the same metadata.name replaces its local counterpart
The system's components are generated from chapter 3's declaration; the staged set under obj/ is inspectable, but regenerated on every start
Code and component names are identical in both modes; only the backing changes

Registration pattern: every command is a package-level `var xxxCmd = &cobra.Command{…}` in `package main` under `cmd/intropy/`, attached to its parent in that file's `func init()`. There is no central registry file — one file per command, plus one file per noun group.

The README's ASCII command tree is at `README.md:162-184` — a new noun must be added there.

Persistent flags (root.go:53-59): `-v/--verbose`, `-q/--quiet`, `--no-color`, `-C/--directory` (chdir in `PersistentPreRunE` root.go:23).

## 2. `int create` end to end

**Flags** — `cmd/intropy/int_create.go:85-99`, struct `createFlags` at :13:
- `-o/--output` (dest dir), `-n/--name`, `--version` (release tag), `-f/--values` (repeatable, `-`=stdin), `-s/--set key=value` (repeatable), `--force`, `--no-input`, `--output-json`, `--install-skills`/`--skip-install-skills` (mutually exclusive :96).
- `Args: cobra.ExactArgs(1)` — the template directory name; `MarkFlagsOneRequired("output","name")` :98.

**Name handling** — `resolveCreateName` (int_create.go:71-83): `-n` is sugar for `--set name=<v>` and defaults `-o` to it; `-n` + `--set name=` is a `usageError`. `-o` is literal, never nested (`dotnet new` semantics; test at `cmd/intropy/int_create_test.go:23`). **There is no PascalCase/kebab-case conversion in Go.** All case derivation lives in the templates' `spec.values` via sprig — e.g. `appId: '{{ .name | kebabcase | replace "." "-" }}'` (`…/intropy-templates/extractor/template.yaml:46`) and `projectName: '{{ .name | replace "-" " " | title | replace " " "" }}'` (`…/intropy-templates/system-host/template.yaml:33`). If `sys create` needs a `pascalCase(name)` in Go it must be written fresh — and the system-host README explicitly requires it to match that sprig expression (`…/system-host/README.md:38-42`).

**Orchestration** — `internal/template/create.go`:
1. `Create(ctx, CreateOptions)` :71; options struct :15, defaults :54.
2. Template source is **GitHub releases**, not Harbor (Harbor is only the skills OCI registry, `int_create_skills.go:21`). Constants `internal/template/github.go:13-19`: owner `integrio-intropy`, repo `intropy-templates`, `template.yaml`, `skeleton`, `https://api.github.com`.
3. `resolveReleaseTag` → `GitHub.LatestTag` (github.go:101) when `--version` empty.
4. `downloadTemplate` (github.go:74) — `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{tag}`, extracted to a temp dir via `ExtractTarGz` (`internal/template/archive.go`); returns `<tmp>/<templateName>` + cleanup.
5. `prepareCreateTemplate` :142 → `LoadTemplate` (`internal/template/manifest.go:167`, validates `apiVersion: intropy.dev/v1`, `kind: Template`) → `Resolve` (`internal/template/values.go:34`).
6. Value layering — `ResolveLayered` (values.go:43): schema defaults → `base` seed → `--values` files → `--set` → prompts for missing required (`internal/template/prompt.go`, `AutoPrompter` create.go:255 returns nil when `--no-input` or stdin isn't a TTY) → JSON Schema validation (values.go:202) → `spec.values` derived strings (values.go:135).
7. Render — `renderCreateOutput` :156 → `ensureOutputDir` :210 (refuses non-empty without `--force`) → `Render` (`internal/template/render.go:27`): `text/template` + `sprig.TxtFuncMap()`, `missingkey=error`; path segments always templated, contents only for `*.tmpl` (suffix stripped), atomic writes (render.go:115).
8. Dependencies — `processDependencies` (`internal/template/dependencies.go:43`), rendered from the same tarball, no prompting, `--force` never propagates, idempotent skip when target already has a matching scaffold record (`dependencyDirScaffold` :171).
9. `WriteScaffold` (create.go:116).
10. `maybeWriteCreateResult` :167 → `CreateResult` (:40, JSON keys `template/owner/repo/version/outputDir/values/dependencies`).
11. Back in the cmd layer: `maybeInstallSkills` (`cmd/intropy/int_create_skills.go:55`).

## 3. `.intropy/scaffold.json`

All in `internal/template/scaffold.go`:

- Constants :11-30 — `ScaffoldSchemaVersion = 1`, `ScaffoldRelPath = ".intropy/scaffold.json"`, `TemplateRoleLabel = "intropy.dev/template-role"`, `RoleSharedLibrary = "shared-library"`.
- `type Scaffold` :38-54:

| Go field | JSON key | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `SchemaVersion int` | `schemaVersion` | |
| `Template string` | `template` | **repo directory name**, not `metadata.name` (create.go:114-117) |
| `Owner string` | `owner` | |
| `Repo string` | `repo` | |
| `Version string` | `version` | resolved release tag |
| `Values map[string]any` | `values` | full resolved map incl. `spec.values` derivations |
| `Role string` | `role,omitempty` | from label `intropy.dev/template-role` (`roleFromLabels` :63) |
| `DependsOn []DependencyRecord` | `dependsOn,omitempty` | |

- `DependencyRecord` :58 — `Template string`/`template`, `Dir string`/`dir` (slash-separated, relative, e.g. `../Models`).
- Writer: `WriteScaffold(projectRoot, s)` :68 → `<root>/.intropy/scaffold.json`, `MarshalIndent` 2-space + trailing newline, 0644. Called at create.go:116 (component) and dependencies.go:132 (dependency).
- Readers: `LoadScaffold(path)` :85, `FindScaffold(startDir)` :100 (walks **up**, returns record + project root, `ErrScaffoldNotFound` :32).

**Important gap for `sys create`:** there is **no `blockKind` / `dataFlow` field today**. `grep -rn "block-kind\|data-flow"` over the CLI returns nothing. The templates repo already declares `intropy.dev/block-kind: extractor|loader` and `intropy.dev/data-flow: in|out` (`…/extractor/template.yaml:14-15`, `…/loader/template.yaml:14-15`) and its `CLAUDE.md:92-98` asserts the CLI "records them in `.intropy/scaffold.json`, which `intropy sys create` later assembles" — that recording is unimplemented. Adding two fields (additive, no `schemaVersion` bump per the comment at scaffold.go:12-15) plus a `blockKindFromLabels`-style helper next to `roleFromLabels` is a prerequisite. Note the topic/appId/name data `sys create` needs is already present in `values` (extractor/loader declare `topic`, `name`, `organization`, and derive `appId`, `models`).

## 4. Existing readers / directory-scanning helpers

- **`manifests create` pins to it**: `internal/deploy/create.go:91` `template.FindScaffold(opts.StartDir)`; schemaVersion guard :98; owner/repo/version taken from the record :101-115 with flag overrides; missing-record error message includes a hand-writable minimal JSON :94; scaffold values seeded into the manifest template via `ResolveLayered` and exposed wholesale under the reserved `scaffold` key (`resolveManifestValues` :160-186, const `scaffoldValuesKey = "scaffold"` :32).
- **`int list` scans downward**: `internal/template/scaffold_list.go` — `ListScaffolds(root) (entries []ScaffoldEntry, warnings []error)` :36. `ScaffoldEntry` :24 = `Path string`/`path` + embedded `Scaffold` (flattened into JSON). Walk semantics: `filepath.WalkDir`, skip set `listSkipDirs` :13 (`.git`, `.intropy`, `node_modules`, `bin`, `dist`), `fs.SkipDir` once matched (projects don't nest :63), unreadable/malformed records become warnings not failures. Consumed at `cmd/intropy/int_list.go:41-65`. **This is the discovery primitive `sys create` should reuse** — it already returns role/values per project; add block-kind filtering on top.
- **Dependency-aware reader**: `dependencyDirScaffold` (`internal/template/dependencies.go:171`) — classifies a target dir as "same template → skip", "missing/empty → render", "foreign scaffold or unmanaged non-empty → error". Good precedent for `sys create`'s idempotency on the host directory.

## 5. Layout & conventions

- **Packages** (`CONTRIBUTING.md:216-224`): `cmd/intropy/` = Cobra commands, one file per command + adjacent `_test.go`; `internal/template/` = fetch/validate/describe/render + scaffold record; `internal/deploy/` = manifests generation (thin consumer of `internal/template`); `internal/skill/` + `internal/skill/oci/`. A new noun would follow `internal/deploy`'s shape: `internal/system/` (or similar) with `Create(ctx, CreateOptions) error`, `CreateOptions` carrying `Stdin/Stdout/Stderr/HTTP/UserAgent` + `Owner/Repo/GitHubBaseURL` test overrides, and a `CreateResult` with stable additive JSON. Package doc convention: see `internal/template/doc.go` and the package comment at `internal/deploy/create.go:1-6`.
- **Errors**: wrap with context (`fmt.Errorf("write scaffold record: %w", err)`); `usageError` via `newUsageErrorf` for exit code 2 (`cmd/intropy/errors.go`, mapped in `main.go:16-33`); sentinel errors like `ErrScaffoldNotFound` with `errors.Is` checks (`deploy/create.go:93`); `SilenceUsage`/`SilenceErrors` set once on root (`root.go:21-22`); `RunE` never calls `os.Exit`. Shared `--output` validation helper: `validateOutputFlag` (`root.go:42`).
- **Output**: program output → `cmd.OutOrStdout()`; progress/diagnostics/warnings → `cmd.ErrOrStderr()` (e.g. `fetching %s/%s@%s`, `created %s from …` at create.go:82/98; `warning: …` at int_list.go:43). No logging library; plain `fmt.Fprintf`. Tables via `text/tabwriter` (int_list.go:60). Machine output via `json.Encoder` with `SetIndent("", "  ")` or an `--output-json` file/`-` sentinel. Cancellation: `signal.NotifyContext(cmd.Context(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)` in each long-running `RunE`.
- **Testing patterns**:
  - Cmd-level: execute `rootCmd` in-process with `rootCmd.SetArgs([...])`, buffers wired via helper `resetRootIO` (`cmd/intropy/skills_list_test.go:83`) and `writeFileT` (:94); `t.Chdir(t.TempDir())`; scaffold fixture helper `writeScaffoldT` (`cmd/intropy/int_list_test.go:12`). Full examples: `int_list_test.go`, `root_test.go`.
  - Pure-logic cmd tests: `cmd/intropy/int_create_test.go` (subtests on `resolveCreateName`, asserts `errors.As(err, &ue)` for usage errors).
  - Package-level: `httptest` GitHub stub — `newTemplateServer` (`internal/template/create_test.go:35`) and `newManifestsServer` (`internal/deploy/create_test.go:163`, which deliberately `t.Error`s if `releases/latest` is hit to prove version pinning), tarballs built by `buildTarGz`, injected through `HTTP: srv.Client()`, `Owner/Repo/GitHubBaseURL`. Scaffold fixture via `template.WriteScaffold` + round-trip through `LoadScaffold` so numbers arrive as `float64` (`deploy/create_test.go:181-205`) — a real trap for any code reading `values` numerics.
  - `make check` = fmt + vet + test; `make ci` adds tidy/lint/`-race`.

## Cross-repo context that shapes this work

`…/tooling/intropy-templates/system-host/` **already exists** and is written against `intropy sys create`:
- `template.yaml:16-18` — "renders this template with only `name` and `--no-input`. No other parameter may ever be required"; label `intropy.dev/template-role: system-host` (:13); derives `projectName`, `systemClass`, `pubsub: pubsub` (:29-35).
- `README.md:14-29` — ownership split: skeleton owns `Program.cs`, csproj, `Taskfile.yml`, `launchSettings.json`, docs; skeleton ships **compilable placeholders** `<projectName>System.cs` and `Topics.cs` that **`sys create` codegen overwrites**; codegen alone owns `Apis.cs`, `Connectors.cs`, and the sibling `<projectName>.Contracts/` project (host csproj reference is `Exists`-guarded, `…SystemHost.csproj.tmpl:26-28`).
- Placeholders to be regenerated: `skeleton/{{ .systemClass }}.cs.tmpl` (`ISystemDefinition`, `SystemName`, `Define(SystemBuilder)` with `builder.AddExtractor("…").Publishes(Topics.X)`) and `skeleton/Topics.cs.tmpl` (`TopicRef<T>.Define("pubsub", "orders")`).
- The C# side lives at `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology` (packages `Intropy.Topology.Aspire` / `.Generation` 0.1.0).
- Templates authoring contract: `…/intropy-templates/CLAUDE.md:92-98` (the two load-bearing labels) and `:113-121` (shared-library role has no block-kind).</result>

# Plan: `intropy sys create` (SystemHost scaffolding)

*Working notes — exploration in progress.*

## Source of truth
- Tutorial: http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/ ch. 3 (+ ch. 1, 2, 4 for context)
- Existing `system-host` template: `~/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates/system-host/` (written against `sys create`)

## What the tutorial promises
`intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host`, run from a workspace root containing
integration scaffolds, must:
1. Scan the workspace for `.intropy/scaffold.json` records (extractor/loader scaffolds).
2. Render the `system-host` template (Aspire AppHost skeleton: csproj, Program.cs,
   launchSettings.json, Taskfile.yml).
3. **Codegen** the typed declaration from the assembled records, overwriting skeleton
   placeholders: `<Name>System.cs` (ISystemDefinition + SystemBuilder wiring),
   `Topics.cs` (TopicRef<T>.Define("pubsub", "orders")), contract record (`Order.cs`).
4. Edges derived from shared topics — components publishing/subscribing the same TopicRef.

## Key findings (agent 1: CLI structure)
- Command layout: one file per command in `cmd/intropy/`, noun groups (`int.go`, `manifests.go`).
  New noun `sys` → `cmd/intropy/sys.go` + `cmd/intropy/sys_create.go`; logic package like
  `internal/deploy` → e.g. `internal/system/`.
- Templates come from GitHub releases (`integrio-intropy/intropy-templates` tarball), not Harbor.
  Reuse `internal/template`: `LoadTemplate`, `ResolveLayered`, `Render`, `downloadTemplate`.
- Scaffold record: `internal/template/scaffold.go` — Scaffold{schemaVersion, template, owner,
  repo, version, values, role, dependsOn}. **No blockKind/dataFlow fields yet** — templates repo
  declares labels `intropy.dev/block-kind` + `intropy.dev/data-flow` but CLI doesn't record them.
  → Prerequisite: record these (additive, no schemaVersion bump), helper like `roleFromLabels`.
- Discovery primitive to reuse: `ListScaffolds(root)` in `internal/template/scaffold_list.go`
  (walks down, skips .git/node_modules etc., warnings not failures).
- `manifests create` (`internal/deploy/create.go`) is the shape precedent: FindScaffold pinning,
  CreateOptions with test seams (HTTP, Owner/Repo/GitHubBaseURL), CreateResult JSON.
- No PascalCase→kebab in Go; case derivation lives in template `spec.values` via sprig.
  system-host template derives `projectName`, `systemClass`, `pubsub: pubsub`; requires only `name`.
- system-host README ownership split: skeleton owns Program.cs/csproj/Taskfile/launchSettings;
  **codegen owns** `<projectName>System.cs`, `Topics.cs`, `Apis.cs`, `Connectors.cs`, sibling
  `<projectName>.Contracts/` project (Exists-guarded csproj ref).
- Values trap: scaffold.json round-trips numbers as float64.
- Testing: httptest GitHub stub (`newTemplateServer`), rootCmd in-process tests, `make check`.

## Open questions (for user)
- TBD after agent 2 (templates/topology) reports.

# 1. Integration templates: location, format, extractor/loader parameters

**Local repo (git), not OCI.** Templates live in a plain git repo `integrio-intropy/intropy-templates`, checked out at `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates`. The CLI fetches them over the **GitHub API** (tarball of a release tag), not from Harbor:

`/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli/internal/template/github.go:13-19`
```go
defaultTemplateOwner = "integrio-intropy"
defaultTemplateRepo  = "intropy-templates"
templateManifestName = "template.yaml"
templateSkeletonDir  = "skeleton"
githubAPIBaseURL     = "https://api.github.com"
```
Harbor (`harbor.intropy.io`) is used only for **skills** OCI artifacts (`cmd/intropy/int_create_skills.go:21`) and platform service images — never for templates.

**On-disk layout** — one directory per template, only two paths are read by the renderer:
```
intropy-templates/
├── extractor/      template.yaml + skeleton/ + README.md + examples/
├── loader/
├── transactional/
├── hello-world/
├── shared-models/
└── system-host/     ← already exists (see §4)
```
Rules (from `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates/CLAUDE.md:30-135`): only `<template>/template.yaml` is parsed, only `<template>/skeleton/` is walked; `.tmpl` suffix means "render contents" (suffix stripped); path segments are always templated; no shared skeleton content between templates.

**Manifest Go structs**: `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli/internal/template/manifest.go` — `Template{APIVersion,Kind,Metadata,Spec}`, `Spec{Parameters map[string]any (raw JSON Schema), Values map[string]string, Dependencies []DependencySpec}`, plus `FieldSpec` as the prompter view. `APIVersionV1 = "intropy.dev/v1"`, `KindTemplate = "Template"`.

**Yes, `extractor` and `loader` both exist**, both declaring `name`, `organization`, `topic` as required plus optional `empty`. Example manifest — `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates/extractor/template.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: intropy.dev/v1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: extractor
  title: Extractor Integration
  labels:
    intropy.io/template-level: example
    intropy.dev/block-kind: extractor
    intropy.dev/data-flow: "in"
spec:
  parameters:
    type: object
    required: [name, organization, topic]
    properties:
      name:        { type: string, pattern: "^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*(\\.[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)*$" }
      organization:{ type: string, pattern: "^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*$" }
      topic:       { type: string, pattern: "^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$" }
      empty:       { type: boolean, default: false }
  values:
    appId: '{{ .name | kebabcase | replace "." "-" }}'
    models: 'Models'
  dependencies:
    - template: shared-models
      output: '{{ .models }}'
      values: { name: '{{ .models }}', empty: '{{ .empty }}' }
```
`loader/template.yaml` is identical in shape with `block-kind: loader`, `data-flow: "out"`.

`shared-models` is the contract-record template: `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates/shared-models/skeleton/Order.cs.tmpl` emits `public record Order(string OrderId, string CustomerId, DateTimeOffset OrderDate, IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines);` into a sibling `Models/` project, referenced by `../../{{ .models }}/{{ .models }}.csproj`.

# 2. What extractor/loader record about pub/sub — and the gap

**Recorded today** (`/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli/internal/template/scaffold.go`):
```go
type Scaffold struct {
	SchemaVersion int            `json:"schemaVersion"`  // = 1
	Template      string         `json:"template"`       // "extractor" | "loader" | ...
	Owner, Repo, Version string
	Values        map[string]any `json:"values"`         // name, organization, topic, empty, appId, models
	Role          string         `json:"role,omitempty"` // ONLY from intropy.dev/template-role
	DependsOn     []DependencyRecord `json:"dependsOn,omitempty"` // {template, dir}
}
```
Written at `internal/template/create.go:116-125`; `Role` comes from `roleFromLabels()` which reads **only** `TemplateRoleLabel = "intropy.dev/template-role"`.

So:
- **`topic`** — yes, recorded (it's a required parameter, so it lands in `Values`).
- **`organization`** — yes, in `Values`.
- **pubsub component name** — **no**. It is hardcoded `"pubsub"` in the skeleton (`extractor/skeleton/src/Configuration/Constants.cs.tmpl`: `public const string PubSubName = "pubsub";` and `local/dapr-components/pubsub.yaml` name: `pubsub`) and re-derived by `system-host`'s `spec.values.pubsub: 'pubsub'`. Not a parameter, not in the record.
- **`blockKind`** — **NOT recorded.** This is a real gap. `intropy-templates/CLAUDE.md:92-98` asserts:

  > "**Two labels are load-bearing.** The CLI reads `intropy.dev/block-kind` … and `intropy.dev/data-flow` … at render time and records them in the scaffolded project's `.intropy/scaffold.json`, which `intropy sys create` later assembles into the system declaration."

  `grep -rn "block-kind\|blockKind\|data-flow"` over `*.go` in intropy-cli returns **zero hits**. The labels exist in the manifests but the CLI drops them. Today `sys create` would have to infer kind from `Scaffold.Template` (`"extractor"` → `AddExtractor`), or the record needs `blockKind`/`dataFlow` fields added (additive → no `ScaffoldSchemaVersion` bump needed per the comment at `scaffold.go:12-16`).

Discovery side is already built: `internal/template/scaffold_list.go` `ListScaffolds(root)` walks the tree and returns `[]ScaffoldEntry{Path, Scaffold}`, skipping `.git/.intropy/node_modules/bin/dist`, not descending into matched dirs — exactly the workspace scan `sys create` needs. Exposed today as `intropy int list --output json` (`cmd/intropy/int_list.go`). `RoleSharedLibrary = "shared-library"` already lets you filter `Models/` out of the block set.

Also note: no `sys`/`sysCmd` exists in the CLI yet (`cmd/intropy/` has `int`, `manifests`, `skills`, `version`, `completions`), and `README.md` has no `sys` mention.

# 3. The .NET topology library

**Location:** `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology` (repo `integrio-intropy/intropy-topology`, net10.0, `Intropy.Topology.slnx`).

**Three NuGet packages** (IDs = project names):
| Project | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Intropy.Topology` | the DSL/model (no external deps) |
| `Intropy.Topology.Generation` | `generate`/`check`/`graph` verbs → Dapr YAML + per-component config |
| `Intropy.Topology.Aspire` | Aspire run backend (`Aspire.Hosting`, `Aspire.Hosting.Redis`, `CommunityToolkit.Aspire.Hosting.Dapr`, `Microcks.Aspire`) |

The system-host template pins `Intropy.Topology.Aspire` / `.Generation` at `Version="0.1.0"` with the comment "must be resolvable from your NuGet feed."

**No `topology.intropy.io/v1` schema exists** — `grep -rn "topology.intropy.io"` over the repo returns nothing. The model's serialized form is the `SystemTopology` JSON emitted by `graph` (`src/Intropy.Topology/Model/SystemTopology.cs`), with no apiVersion/kind envelope. The only `intropy.dev/v1` apiVersion in the workspace is the template manifest.

**`ISystemDefinition`** — `/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/Intropy.Topology/src/Intropy.Topology/Discovery.cs`:
```csharp
public interface ISystemDefinition
{
    string SystemName { get; }
    void Define(SystemBuilder builder);
}
```
`SystemDiscovery.Discover(Assembly)` requires **exactly one** concrete implementation per assembly (throws on 0 or >1) and needs a parameterless ctor. Load-bearing for `sys create`: if codegen's PascalCase derivation ever disagrees with the template's, you get two `ISystemDefinition`s and discovery throws — the system-host manifest calls this out explicitly.

**`SystemBuilder`** — `src/Intropy.Topology/SystemBuilder.cs`: `static Create(string systemName)` (DNS-1123 label), `AddExtractor/AddAggregator/AddLoader/AddTransactionalIntegration(name)` returning per-kind builders, then `Build()` / `TryBuild(out topology, out diagnostics)` / `Validate()`. **There is no `AddTopic`** — topics/connectors/services materialize from usage.

Builder edge methods (`src/Intropy.Topology/Building/ComponentBuilders.cs`): `ExtractorBuilder.From(ConnectorRef)` + `.Publishes(TopicRef)` / `.Publishes(string port, TopicRef)`; `LoaderBuilder.Subscribes(TopicRef)` + `.To(ConnectorRef)`; `AggregatorBuilder.Subscribes(params TopicRef[])` + `.Publishes(...)`; `TransactionalIntegrationBuilder.Provides/From/To`.

**`TopicRef`** — `src/Intropy.Topology/Refs.cs`:
```csharp
public abstract record TopicRef {
    public string PubSubName { get; }   // DNS-1123 subdomain
    public string TopicName  { get; }
    public abstract Type ContractType { get; }
}
public sealed record TopicRef<T> : TopicRef {
    public static TopicRef<T> Define([ConstantExpected] string pubSubName,
                                     [ConstantExpected] string topicName) => new(pubSubName, topicName);
}
```
Note `[ConstantExpected]` — generated code must pass literals. Same file also has `ApiRef<T>.Define(name)`, `ConnectorRef.Define(name[, ExternalSystem[, Transport]])` (three overloads; the name-only one is documented as "the form a block scaffold emits", unresolved → warning ITP107 resolved at "`intropy system create`"), `ExternalSystem`, and `Transport` (`Http`/`Sftp`/`Blob`/`Custom`).

**Both entry points exist and are implemented:**
- `Intropy.Topology.Aspire/IntropyAspire.cs:31` — `public static async Task<int> RunAsync(Assembly assembly, string[] args)` (discovers → generates dev artifacts to temp → builds Aspire graph → `app.RunAsync()`)
- `Intropy.Topology.Generation/IntropyGenerate.cs:20` — `public static Task<int> RunAsync(Assembly assembly, string[] args)`

Tests exist for both: `test/Intropy.Topology.Aspire.Test/IntropyAspireTests.cs`, `test/Intropy.Topology.Generation.Test/IntropyGenerateTests.cs`.

# 4. A `system-host` template already exists

`/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates/system-host/` (dated 25 Jul 09:02) is written **specifically for `intropy sys create`** and already contains every file you listed.

`system-host/template.yaml`:
```yaml

  name: system-host
  description: The Aspire host project of an Intropy integration system. … Scaffolded by
    `intropy sys create`, whose codegen assembles the declaration files (the system definition,

  labels:

  # or a `spec.values` derivation.
  parameters:
    type: object
    required: [name]
```

2. **PascalCase must match:** `spec.values.projectName` comments — *"Must keep matching the CLI's pascalCase(name): codegen overwrites `<projectName>System.cs` — if the derivations disagree, codegen adds a second ISystemDefinition next to the placeholder"*. <ProjectReference Include="../{{ .projectName }}.Contracts/{{ .projectName }}.Contracts.csproj"


options.label: Derive from topic name

options.label: All block kinds
options.description: Also handle transactional integrations and aggregators (Subscribes/Publishes joins), plus connector refs. Bigger surface, more edge cases, ahead of tutorial coverage.

content.content:
===== 01-extractor =====
1. The extractor¶
In this chapter you create the system workspace, scaffold the first of its two integrations, and run it alone: a complete integration on its own isolated components, before any system exists.
Scaffold¶
Create the workspace and render the extractor blueprint into it:
```
mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow
intropy int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor
```
order-flow/ is the system workspace: a plain directory that holds the two integrations and, from chapter 3, the SystemHost as siblings. Nothing about it is special. Each integration stays an independent project you could version, test, and deploy on its own.
Two flags deserve a closer look:
-s topic=orders: the pub/sub topic the extractor publishes to. You'll type the same value when scaffolding the loader — each scaffold declares its own half of the contract, and records it (in .intropy/scaffold.json) for the system to assemble in chapter 3.
No empty=true: unlike the transactional tutorial, you keep the blueprint's sample logic. This tutorial is about what happens between integrations, so the insides stay stock.
The render's last line reports a project you didn't ask for: created dependency Models from template shared-models. The workspace now holds two directories:
```
order-flow/
├── Models/                       # shared contract types — scaffolded once per workspace
│   ├── Models.csproj
│   ├── Order.cs                  # the order contract the extractor publishes
│   └── OrderLine.cs
└── order-extractor/
    ├── Taskfile.yml              # task run / build / test
    ├── docker-compose.yml        # local observability stack — standalone runs only
    ├── local/
    │   ├── dapr-components/
    │   │   ├── poll.yaml         # cron binding — sweeps the inbound folder every 5 s
    │   │   ├── inbound.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the source system
    │   │   └── pubsub.yaml       # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
    │   └── sample-data/
    │       └── sample-order.json
    ├── src/                      # implemented: sweep inbound, transform, publish
    └── test/
```
The extractor itself looks like the transactional layout you know, with its own components. Models/ is new: the extractor template declares the shared-models template as a dependency, so scaffolding the first block into a workspace also scaffolds the workspace's contract library next to it. It holds the Order record (and its OrderLine lines): the shape the extractor publishes, defined in neither block because both halves of the system need it. The extractor references it as an ordinary ProjectReference (../../Models/Models.csproj); its own source shape stays private in src/Model/In.cs, and the pipeline's transform step maps that In to the shared Order before publishing.
The sample logic ships working. On every poll tick it lists the inbound folder, publishes each file's content as an Order message on topic orders, and deletes the source file. And unlike the transactional integration, which runs once and exits, the extractor keeps running until you stop it — that matters in chapter 5, when you'll drop files in while the whole system is live.
Check it¶
Run the extractor standalone:
```
cd order-extractor
task run
```
The task seeds sample-order.json into the inbound folder and starts the integration under Dapr, with the sidecar loading only local/dapr-components/. Within a poll tick you should see:
```
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Swept 1 file from inbound
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Stop it with Ctrl+C, then confirm the source file is gone:
```
ls local/storage/inbound/
```
The folder is empty: the extractor swept the file, published it, and cleaned up.
Where did the message go? Into the extractor's own in-memory pub/sub — and nothing subscribes there. That's the point of an isolated run: it verifies the extractor's whole job (sweep, publish, clean up) without needing a consumer to exist. Delivery to a consumer is the system's job, and that's chapter 5.
Recap
Created the order-flow workspace; integrations and the SystemHost live in it as siblings
Scaffolded order-extractor from the extractor blueprint with its sample logic intact
The render also scaffolded Models/, the workspace's shared contract library — the Order record the extractor publishes lives there, not in the extractor
Standalone, the sidecar loads only local/dapr-components/: an isolated, in-memory world
The published message intentionally went nowhere — no consumer exists yet
===== 02-loader =====
2. The loader¶
In this chapter you scaffold order-loader, the consuming half of the system, and verify it the way any subscriber is verified in isolation: by publishing through its own sidecar.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root, render the loader blueprint:
```
intropy int create loader -n OrderLoader -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-loader
```
-s topic=orders is the same value you gave the extractor, and typing it twice is deliberate: each integration declares its own half of the contract and stays verifiable alone. Chapter 3 assembles the two halves into one typed declaration — and checks that they meet.
The message shape, though, is not typed twice. The loader template declares the same shared-models dependency as the extractor, and this time the render finds the project already in place:
```
dependency Models already scaffolded from shared-models — skipped
```
The first block into a workspace creates Models/; every later one detects it by its scaffold record and reuses it. Both blocks now compile against the same Order record, so the shape of the messages crossing the system has exactly one definition.
```
order-loader/
├── Taskfile.yml
├── docker-compose.yml
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/
│       ├── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│       └── destination.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the destination system
├── src/                          # implemented: subscribe to topic, deserialize, validate, load
└── test/
```
The sample logic subscribes to orders on pubsub and, for each message, deserializes it into the shared Order record, validates it, and writes {orderId}.json through the destination binding. The mirror image of the extractor's shape handling: the loader consumes the shared Order and maps it to its own private destination shape in src/Model/Out.cs. Like the extractor, it runs until you stop it.
Note that pubsub.yaml here has the same component name as the extractor's — but they are not the same broker. Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.
Publish through the loader's own sidecar¶
A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists inside the loader's sidecar, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and dapr publish --publish-app-id does exactly that.
Start the loader in one terminal:
```
cd order-loader
task run
```
Wait for the subscription to register:
```
== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Check it¶
In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:
```
dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
```
```
Event published successfully
```
The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:
```
cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json
```
```
{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}
```
Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.
Recap
Scaffolded order-loader: subscribes to orders on pubsub, writes each order through the destination binding
The loader's render found Models/ already scaffolded and skipped it — both blocks compile against one shared Order record
A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet
===== 03-systemhost =====
3. The SystemHost¶
In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root:
```
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
```
The noun is sys, not int, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: OrderFlow
kebab-cases to order-flow, the system's name.
The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with -s topic=orders, in
.intropy/scaffold.json — and sys create scans the workspace for those records and assembles
them into a typed declaration. Models/ has a record too, marked as a shared library rather than
a block, so the host reads it as the contract project: referenced, never declared as a component.
```
system-host/
├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
├── Properties/
│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
```
One thing is conspicuously absent: a dapr-components/ directory. The system's components are not
files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
watches that happen.
One entry point, two backends¶
system-host/Program.cs
```
using System.Reflection;
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```
Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.
The declaration¶
Open Topics.cs. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
system-host/Topics.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
using Models;
/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```
OrderFlowSystem.cs is the topology itself:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```
Nothing in these files is new information. AddExtractor and AddLoader name the blueprints you
scaffolded; "pubsub" and "orders" are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What sys create did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.
Three things about the shape:
A topic is a value, not a string typed twice: Topics.Orders is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
The edge is derived: no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching Topics.Orders is the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
Block kinds surface at the host: the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  Publishes but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
And one thing about what is not declared: a pub/sub registration. Topics.Orders names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.
Order, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries: the same record from the
workspace's Models/ library that the extractor's transform step produces and the loader's
deserializer consumes. sys create recognized the library by its scaffold record and referenced
it from the host instead of generating a contract of its own, so the declaration doesn't just say
that both ends touch a topic named orders — it carries the very type both compile against. The
wiring itself only uses the names; the type documents the contract at the declaration site and
gives schema-aware tooling something to reflect on.
Declared, then enforced¶
A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and Build() is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run check, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.
Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```
```
dotnet run -- check
```
```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```
Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to Topics.Orders.
How the declaration reaches the code¶
The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.
Info
The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, sys create
assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.
Check it¶
```
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```
```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```
check builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:
```
dotnet run -- graph
```
```
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```
That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.
Recap
sys create assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: Topics.cs defines
  each topic once, typed with the shared Order record from Models/, and
  OrderFlowSystem.cs wires components to it
The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing Topics.Orders; block kinds at the host
  mirror the blueprints
Build() validates the whole declaration; dotnet run -- check runs the same gate from the
  command line
dotnet run -- graph prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet

===== 03-systemhost =====
3. The SystemHost¶
In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root:
```
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
```
The noun is sys, not int, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: OrderFlow
kebab-cases to order-flow, the system's name.
The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with -s topic=orders, in
.intropy/scaffold.json — and sys create scans the workspace for those records and assembles
them into a typed declaration. Models/ has a record too, marked as a shared library rather than
a block, so the host reads it as the contract project: referenced, never declared as a component.
```
system-host/
├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
├── Properties/
│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
```
One thing is conspicuously absent: a dapr-components/ directory. The system's components are not
files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
watches that happen.
One entry point, two backends¶
system-host/Program.cs
```
using System.Reflection;
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```
Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.
The declaration¶
Open Topics.cs. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
system-host/Topics.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
using Models;
/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```
OrderFlowSystem.cs is the topology itself:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```
Nothing in these files is new information. AddExtractor and AddLoader name the blueprints you
scaffolded; "pubsub" and "orders" are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What sys create did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.
Three things about the shape:
A topic is a value, not a string typed twice: Topics.Orders is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
The edge is derived: no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching Topics.Orders is the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
Block kinds surface at the host: the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  Publishes but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
And one thing about what is not declared: a pub/sub registration. Topics.Orders names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.
Order, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries: the same record from the
workspace's Models/ library that the extractor's transform step produces and the loader's
deserializer consumes. sys create recognized the library by its scaffold record and referenced
it from the host instead of generating a contract of its own, so the declaration doesn't just say
that both ends touch a topic named orders — it carries the very type both compile against. The
wiring itself only uses the names; the type documents the contract at the declaration site and
gives schema-aware tooling something to reflect on.
Declared, then enforced¶
A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and Build() is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run check, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.
Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```
```
dotnet run -- check
```
```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```
Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to Topics.Orders.
How the declaration reaches the code¶
The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.
Info
The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, sys create
assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.
Check it¶
```
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```
```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```
check builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:
```
dotnet run -- graph
```
```
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```
That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.
Recap
sys create assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: Topics.cs defines
  each topic once, typed with the shared Order record from Models/, and
  OrderFlowSystem.cs wires components to it
The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing Topics.Orders; block kinds at the host
  mirror the blueprints
Build() validates the whole declaration; dotnet run -- check runs the same gate from the
  command line
dotnet run -- graph prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet
